What happened? Just look at them.
Hello, dear Victoria Sergeevna!
Very funny, what is going on here, Max?
Is this a tavern we are running here or what?
Why are the two of you drinking in here?
Well, what can I possibly do?
In short, let us go with this plan.
Right now I will get him drunk quickly.
Careful they do not have to resuscitate you instead.
Well, we will see about that.
Chef, let us drink like real men!

meanings.note: Prefix 'из-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'винить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'excuse me', paired with 'извинять'.

examples.trans: Excuse me, here is your change.
Excuse me, I did not have time to change clothes.
Excuse me, I forgot again today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What am I doing here?
How did I end up here?
Alright, that is it, I am leaving now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There is nothing left to drink together!
We have nothing at home.
Of course you can, let us go cure our hangover.

meanings.en: to make it, to be in time
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'спеть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'managed', paired with 'успевать'.

examples.trans: Excuse me, I did not have time to change clothes.
I didn't manage to call.
We'll make it! The president always talks for a long time.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'одеться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to change clothes'.

related.gloss: not to to change clothes (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: Excuse me, I did not have time to change clothes.

examples.text: Надо заехать домой, принять душ, переодеться.
examples.trans: I need to stop by home, take a shower, change.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What am I doing here?
We will find something to drink now.

examples.text: Я вижу, что у неё выходной.
examples.trans: I can see that she has a day off.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лучиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'happened', paired with 'случаться'.

examples.trans: What happened?
Nothing will happen.

examples.text: Марина, я вам обещаю: со стеной ничего не случится.
examples.trans: Marina, I promise you: nothing will happen to the wall.

meanings.en: to have a look, to take a look
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'смотреть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'look', paired with 'смотреть'.

examples.trans: I looked over the contract with the meatpacking plant.
May I have a look?
I only had a look.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Maxim knows, this is his room.
We will find something to drink now.
We have nothing at home.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'them', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Они там что-то со сроками мутят.
examples.trans: They are scheming something with the deadlines there.

examples.text: Они связывают нас с другими людьми.
examples.trans: They connect us with other people.
They are building a centre.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'hello'.

examples.trans: Hello, Chef, how are things?

examples.text: Здравствуйте, а у Насти сегодня выходной.
examples.trans: Hello, Nastya has a day off today.
Hello, dear Victoria Sergeevna!

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'рогой'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('dear').

examples.trans: Hello, dear Victoria Sergeevna!
Hey there, hello, my dear Kostya!
These are expensive clothes.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Не хочешь взять деньги, тогда заработай.
examples.trans: If you do not want to take money, then earn it.
He gets very bored being alone there.
Buddy, I really need you right now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мешно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Очень смешно, что за дела, Макс?
examples.trans: Very funny, what is going on here, Max?
Do you find it funny?
That's very funny.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How did I end up here?
Of course, we will definitely get married.
I am actually finishing law school soon.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'things to do' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: What am I doing here?
Hello, Chef, how are things?
This is none of my business, of course.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, near, with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello, Chef, how are things?
There is nothing left to drink together!
Alright, that is it, I am leaving now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'us', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Of course, we will definitely get married.

examples.text: Вообще-то мы сейчас на свадьбу копим.
examples.trans: Actually, we are saving up for the wedding right now.
We want to do everything ourselves.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Нет, я не могу тут работать.
examples.trans: No, I cannot work here.
Well, do you like it here?
Barinov is here, he called for me.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'tavern, pub' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У нас тут кабак, что ли?
examples.trans: Is this a tavern we are running here or what?

examples.text: На кухне ресторана всегда есть кабак.
examples.trans: In the restaurant kitchen there is always tavern.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'whether', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Get ready, let us go cure this hangover together.
Of course you can, let us go cure our hangover.

examples.text: Шеф, вы же ничего не говорили.
examples.trans: Chef, you did not say anything about money.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (polite/plural)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There is nothing left to drink together!
We will find something to drink now.

examples.text: Здравствуйте, а у Насти сегодня выходной.
examples.trans: Hello, Nastya has a day off today.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'чему').

examples.text: А ты почему ещё в форме?
examples.trans: And why are you still in your uniform?
Why are the two of you drinking in here?
Why are we going so slowly?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What am I doing here?
How did I end up here?
What on earth is going on here right now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'the two of us, together (two)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Why are the two of you drinking in here?
The two of us live together.
Let's celebrate just the two of us.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'are drinking', paired with 'выпить'.

related.gloss: to go on a drinking binge

examples.trans: There is nothing left to drink together!
We will find something to drink now.

examples.text: Я не буду тут один пить!
examples.trans: I am not going to drink here alone!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, well', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мне на заводе хороший юрист нужен.
examples.trans: I need a capable lawyer at my factory.
I need a lawyer at the factory.
Well, do you like it here?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What am I doing here?
Maxim knows, this is his room.
Hello, Chef, how are things?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, am able to', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: Kostya, I really want to help you.
But you have to help me with it.

examples.text: Ты должна мне в этом помочь.
examples.trans: You must help me with this.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'делать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'делать'.

examples.trans: We want to do everything ourselves.

examples.text: Ну а что я могу сделать?
examples.trans: Well, what can I possibly do?
In short, let us go with this plan.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'long story short', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I am actually finishing law school soon.
In short, let us go with this plan.
In short, I have a plan.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

related.gloss: to give (the verb it comes from)

examples.trans: Let me try working here for now.
Well alright, let us keep playing.
Take off that suit jacket quickly.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'such, what sort', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Alright, that is it, I am leaving now.

examples.text: Не каждый день предлагают такую работу.
examples.trans: They do not offer a job like this every day.

examples.text: Бери такси и приезжай ко мне.
examples.trans: Take a taxi and come to me.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'plan' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: What are your plans going forward?
In short, let us go with this plan.
In short, I have a plan.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: We will find something to drink now.

examples.text: Вообще-то мы сейчас на свадьбу копим.
examples.trans: Actually, we are saving up for the wedding right now.
What on earth is going on here right now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'his', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Of course you can, let us go cure our hangover.
This is none of my business, of course.
Of course, we will definitely get married.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Alright, then come in here quickly.
Take off that suit jacket quickly.
Right now I will get him drunk quickly.

meanings.en: to give drink to, hydrate, intoxicate
meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'поить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'I will get him drunk'.

related.gloss: to I will get him drunk (prefixed perfective)
not to I will get him drunk (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: They decided to give the guest tea to drink.

examples.text: Раз не можем напоить, мы его накормим!
examples.trans: Since we cannot give him drink, we will feed him!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello, Chef, how are things?
How did I end up here?
What are your plans going forward?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'would', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Just to become a notary in some backwater?
The next stage of friendship awaits you.
Alright, then come in here quickly.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Are you planning to marry Nastya?
Do you think about the future at all?
Well that is it, pal, you are trapped now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'качивать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to resuscitate, to pump out'.

examples.text: Как бы тебя откачивать не пришлось.
examples.trans: Careful they do not have to resuscitate you instead.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и откачивать вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and to resuscitate on time.

meanings.en: to have to, to be forced to
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'йтись'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'had to, it fell to', paired with 'приходиться'.

examples.trans: I'm going to have to torture you.
We had to wait a long time.

examples.text: Ты что, очкарик, не понимаешь? Мне тебя мучить придётся.
examples.trans: Don't you get it, four-eyes? I'm going to have to torture you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Maxim knows, this is his room.
This is none of my business, of course.
And just when will that happen?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'else/more', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: He has not arrived yet.

examples.text: Хорошо, я ещё вещи не разобрала.
examples.trans: Alright, I have not unpacked my things yet.

examples.text: А он у Лёвы живёт ещё?
examples.trans: And is he still living at Lyova's place?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'let's', paired with 'дать'.

examples.trans: Let me try working here for now.
Well alright, let us keep playing.
Take off that suit jacket quickly.

meanings.en: to drink up, to have a drink
meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'пить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'let's drink', paired with 'выпивать'.

examples.trans: There is nothing left to drink together!
We will find something to drink now.
Oh, I've had a bit to drink now.

meanings.en: in a masculine way, like a real man
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem '-мужски').

examples.trans: Chef, let us drink like real men!
Like a real man, for about ten seconds.
He acted like a real man.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'there is'.

examples.text: Можно же просто напиться и забыть.
examples.trans: Of course, you can just get drunk and forget.
I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
